bottom_line: Prices are still rising and the Fed (the people who set interest rates) is now openly talking about raising rates again in December. Stocks just had a big comeback week, but money for borrowing and everyday stuff is still getting more expensive.

stories.title: Rate hike talk is back
stories.real: Inflation (prices going up) has hit a 3-year high, and the chances of a December rate hike are rising. The economy is also growing faster than expected, so the Fed has less reason to wait.
stories.you: If rates go up, loans, credit cards and mortgages cost more. The 30-year mortgage rate is already at 7.21%.

stories.title: Stocks bounce back hard
stories.real: After a November sell-off pushed the S&P 500 into a correction (a drop of about 10% from its high), stocks roared back. The Dow rose 592 points on Black Friday, and it was the S&P 500's best week in 19 months, led by AI stocks like Nvidia and Micron.

stories.title: Holiday budgets are getting squeezed
stories.real: Food, travel and gifts all cost more this year, and even toys are going up. Higher energy costs from the Iran war are part of why, and the average new car hit $51,109 in October.
stories.you: Your paycheck buys less this holiday season, so a lot of families are cutting back.

stories.title: Trump disputes GDP numbers
stories.real: The government revised its third-quarter GDP number (the total value of everything the economy makes) way up. President Trump called it a mistake and demanded an investigation.
stories.you: A stronger economy on paper gives the Fed more room to raise rates, and that hits what you pay to borrow.

stories.title: Jobs report is next
stories.real: Next week brings new hiring data, which will weigh heavily on what the Fed does in December. There are already signs of growth without many new jobs.
stories.you: If hiring is weak, getting a raise or switching jobs gets harder even while prices keep climbing.
